This report provides a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework in Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's flagship innovation incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—delivers more than $4 billion annually in tax relief through a dual statutory mechanism: an immediate 100% income deduction (or indefinite pool carryforward) under Section 37 of the ITA, and a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA. Between December 2024 and November 2026, the federal and provincial R&D landscape underwent its most expansive statutory overhaul in over a decade. Enacted via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), the federal government doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (generating up to $2,100,000 in annual refundable federal credits), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Furthermore, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review service standards in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. Most recently, Budget 2026 (tabled on November 5, 2026, by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, as analysed by Kreston GTA) proposed a $930 million five-year expansion of the SR&ED program—which would apply to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (Budget Day)—to cover post-prototype product/process certification and validation costs as well as intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs, alongside the proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction, which would allow a 100% first-year write-off for eligible depreciable property acquired on or after September 15, 2026. Concurrently, major provincial reforms—most notably Québec's consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) offering 30% and 20% fully refundable rates for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and British Columbia's Budget 2026 legislation (Bill 2) making the 10% BC SR&ED tax credit permanent and matching the $6,000,000 federal expenditure cap—have fundamentally reshaped multi-jurisdictional R&D tax planning across Canada.
Section 1: Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 The Dual-Incentive Statutory Framework (Section 37 and Sections 127 / 127.1)

Canada's federal SR&ED program is codified within the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and Part XXIX (Section 2900 et seq.) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Unlike single-stage R&D tax regimes, calculating an SR&ED claim in Canada requires two related but legally distinct statutory computations that should never be treated as interchangeable in audit working papers.

First, Section 37 of the ITA governs the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Subsection 37(1) establishes a cumulative expenditure pool that permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada directly against business income in the taxation year incurred, or to carry forward any undeducted pool balance indefinitely to reduce business income in future taxation years. Within subsection 37(1), paragraph 37(1)(a) governs expenditures of a current nature, including salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), and third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii). Following the enactment of Bill C-15, newly restored paragraph 37(1)(b) re-establishes the deductibility of capital expenditures made on depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, for SR&ED carried on in Canada, where the SR&ED is directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and relates to the taxpayer's business. Furthermore, under subsection 37(1.1), if a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (such as a wholly owned R&D subsidiary performing research for its parent corporation's active business), the SR&ED is deemed to relate to the claimant's business.

Second, Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA govern Qualified Expenditures and the Investment Tax Credit (ITC). Once allowable SR&ED expenditures are determined under Section 37, subsection 127(9) defines the "qualified expenditure" base and the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" used to earn federal ITCs. Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of earned ITCs against Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, while Section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)) governs the calculation and payment of refundable investment tax credits to qualifying taxpayers whose earned ITCs exceed their Part I tax liabilities.

An expenditure may be 100% deductible under the Section 37 expenditure pool without generating an equivalent qualified expenditure under Section 127. For example, payments to non-arm's length SR&ED contractors, acquisitions of used depreciable capital equipment after December 15, 2024, and unpaid non-wage current expenditures (outstanding more than 180 days after year-end) are included in the Section 37 deductible pool in the year incurred, but are excluded or restricted when computing Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—a notional overhead substitute equal to 55% of the capped SR&ED salary base under ITR subsection 2900(4)—is included in Section 127 qualified expenditures to generate ITCs, yet is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the ITA

The gateway to all federal and harmonized provincial R&D incentives is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED—in general alignment with the OECD Frascati Manual—as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three core research categories—basic research, applied research, or experimental development—alongside commensurate direct support work, while expressly excluding seven enumerated commercial and routine activities.
The CRA's "Why" and "How" Eligibility Framework

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA issued its Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives, replacing the archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy. As confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the 2021 Guidelines did not alter the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) or override the common-law five-question test from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen; rather, they consolidated the statutory and judicial tests into two mandatory foundational requirements—"Why" and "How"—that must both be satisfied for work to qualify.

The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement Driven by Uncertainty) stipulates that the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA clarifies that the sought-after knowledge must be conceptual knowledge (such as underlying principles, theories, or prediction models) rather than purely factual knowledge (such as routine measurements or data points). New scientific or technological knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of publicly available scientific or technological knowledge or the standard practice and existing knowledge of competent professionals in the field (including the combined knowledge within the business and publicly available sources). If a technical obstacle is circumvented via a workaround using existing knowledge, or resolved through routine engineering, on-the-job training, purchasing proprietary know-how, or hiring an external consultant who already possesses the solution, the "Why" requirement is not met. Crucially, commercial success or failure is irrelevant when assessing the "Why" requirement: an experiment that refutes a hypothesis or results in a failed prototype still achieves a technological advancement by expanding the technological knowledge base and establishing why a given approach fails under specific constraints.

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search) dictates that the work must be carried out in a field of science or technology (restricted to the natural sciences and engineering; social sciences and humanities are excluded) through a disciplined, systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis. Merely following standard engineering design methods, business practices, or established procedures in a methodical manner is insufficient for SR&ED eligibility. Instead, under CRA guidelines and appellate jurisprudence, an SR&ED systematic investigation requires a rigorous four-step methodology:

items: Defining the scientific or technological problem and formulating an initial hypothesis—an idea consistent with known facts, expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or testable model, that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the uncertainty.
Planning and testing that hypothesis through controlled experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and be modified iteratively as empirical testing progresses.
Developing logical conclusions grounded directly in the empirical results or analytical findings of the experiments.
Maintaining contemporaneous evidence generated as the investigation progresses to substantiate the hypotheses tested and results obtained.

body.text: Core Research Categories, Support Work, and Statutory Exclusions

Subsection 248(1) structures the scope of SR&ED into paragraphs (a) through (k), which establish the statutory boundary between qualifying research, eligible support work, and non-qualifying commercial operations:

cells: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view (e.g., studying a newly discovered virus to better understand its fundamental molecular characteristics).

Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (e.g., efforts to develop a vaccine against a new virus by exploiting identified characteristics of that virus).

Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto (e.g., scale-up and optimization of processes to enable rapid large-scale vaccine production). Represents the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada.

Work with respect to (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work never qualifies on a standalone basis.
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes.
Research in the social sciences or the humanities.
Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas.
The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Style changes (e.g., cosmetic iterations to a product's form, finish, or aesthetic proportions).

body.text: In evaluating experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work identify seven technical indicators demonstrating that available technological knowledge is insufficient (thereby establishing technological uncertainty): existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; too many variables or unknowns interact simultaneously; parameters or conditions lie outside the normal operating range; the nature of the technical problem is evolving; required engineering data is not readily available; or interlocking system constraints prevent standard component changes. While purely financial or cost targets do not create technological uncertainty on their own, attempting to satisfy stringent cost targets under severe physical or material constraints can impose genuine technological uncertainty.

When distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as data collection or testing) and excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) (routine testing or routine data collection), the CRA evaluates purpose. Data collection performed as a routine activity for quality control or assurance during normal commercial operations is excluded under paragraphs (f) and (k); conversely, data collection executed specifically to test a scientific or technological hypothesis within an active SR&ED experiment qualifies as support work under paragraph (d). Conducting excluded activities (such as prospecting for minerals) alongside eligible SR&ED does not taint the eligible project, provided the excluded work and its costs are segregated and left out of the SR&ED claim.
1.3 Legislative Reforms (2024–2026): FES 2024, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025), and Budget 2026
Tax practitioners and auditors reviewing Canadian R&D claims across the 2024–2027 period must carefully track three sequential waves of federal legislative reform.
1. The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) vs. Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 (Enacted March 26, 2026)

In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and the Department of Finance's August 2025 draft legislative proposals, the federal government initially proposed increasing the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000. However, Budget 2025 (tabled on November 4, 2025) superseded that intermediate figure and doubled the enhanced expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. These enhancements were formally enacted into law through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026.

Under Bill C-15, five structural statutory amendments apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and, for capital property and lease costs, to property acquired or lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024). First, under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6), the maximum annual expenditure limit on which the 35% enhanced ITC can be earned doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Second, under subsection 127(10.2), for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada thresholds over which the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out were raised from $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000.

Third, under subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.6) to (10.64), and 127.1(2.01), eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) throughout the taxation year on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures), subject to a phase-out based on three-year average annual revenue between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Fourth, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) (and consequential continuing-corporation rules in paragraph 87(2)(j.6)), stand-alone CCPCs and associated groups of CCPCs gained an optional election to bypass the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) and instead compute their $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average revenue phase-out structure ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000). Fifth, Bill C-15 repealed the post-2013 capital exclusion rules by adding paragraph 37(1)(b) (alongside amendments to paragraphs 37(1)(d), 37(8)(a), and 37(8)(e), and subsections 37(6), 37(6.1), 127(11.5), and 127.1(2.01)), restoring both the Section 37 income deduction and Section 127 ITC eligibility for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (including All-or-Substantially-All [ASA] capital property and First/Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment [SUE]) and equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024. Consequentially, Bill C-15 repealed the third-party capital look-through rules in subsections 37(14) and 37(15) and repealed paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1).
2. Budget 2026 Expansions (Tabled November 5, 2026)

On November 5, 2026, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled the 2026 Federal Budget, which—as detailed in Kreston GTA's November 9, 2026 budget analysis—proposes two major structural expansions affecting R&D-intensive businesses.

First, Budget 2026 proposes to expand the SR&ED program to include post-prototype commercialization, certification, and IP protection costs. Historically, SR&ED eligibility terminated at the prototype or pilot plant stage once technological uncertainty was resolved, treating subsequent regulatory validation and patenting as ineligible commercial expenses. Allocating $930 million over five years and $235 million per year thereafter—applicable to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (Budget Day)—Budget 2026 would bring two new categories of post-R&D expenditures into the SR&ED regime, provided the underlying product or process was developed through a qualifying SR&ED project:

items: Product and Process Certification and Validation: Covers the costs of tests, technological validations, and studies required to obtain initial regulatory approval or certification for a new product or process developed through eligible SR&ED. Eligible costs fall into standard SR&ED expenditure categories (salaries, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery/equipment), but exclude routine compliance testing, annual surveillance audits, and re-certification triggered by supplier changes.

Intellectual Property (IP) Protection and Maintenance: Covers the costs of registering and maintaining IP protection—including patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software—whether protected in Canada or under equivalent foreign law. While administrative filing and maintenance fees paid to foreign IP offices are eligible, supporting activities (such as patent application drafting and preparation) qualify only if conducted within Canada, and IP enforcement or litigation costs are excluded.

body.text: Second, Budget 2026 confirms the government's intention to implement the permanent Productivity Mega Deduction. Originally announced on September 15, 2026, the Productivity Mega Deduction would allow businesses to deduct up to 100% of the cost of most depreciable capital property in the first taxation year the asset becomes available for use, applying to eligible property acquired on or after September 15, 2026. Estimated by Kreston GTA to cover over 65% of business investment, reduce Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new investment from 13% to 6.4%, and cost $36 billion over five years, the Mega Deduction interacts directly with the restored SR&ED capital rules:

items: Equipment Used ≥90% (ASA) for SR&ED in Canada (such as dedicated lab instruments and test rigs) remains 100% deductible through the Section 37 SR&ED pool (which can be carried forward indefinitely) and earns the 35% SR&ED ITC (40% refundable for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs).

Equipment Used >50% to <90% for SR&ED in Canada (such as shared test equipment or pilot lines) qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), earning a partial SR&ED ITC on up to 50% of its cost over two years (25% per period), while up to 100% of the remaining capital cost could be written off immediately in Year 1 under the Productivity Mega Deduction on Schedule T2SCH8 in place of regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates.

Equipment Used Mainly for Production (≤50% SR&ED) is ineligible for SR&ED credits, but up to 100% of its cost could be written off in Year 1 under the Productivity Mega Deduction. Unlike the Section 37 SR&ED pool (which carries forward indefinitely), the Productivity Mega Deduction could only be claimed in the first taxation year the asset becomes available for use; any unclaimed portion falls back to standard CCA deduction rates in subsequent years.

2.1 Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates and Claimant Categories

Under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA, the rate at which a claimant earns SR&ED ITCs and the proportion of those ITCs that can be refunded in cash depend on the legal classification of the taxpayer, whether the expenditures fall within the corporation's annual expenditure limit, and whether the expenditures are of a current or capital nature.

The Basic ITC Rate of 15% applies to all corporations (other than CCPCs and ECPCs claiming within their expenditure limit), sole proprietorships (individuals), trusts, and partnerships on all qualified SR&ED expenditures (measured as the excess of the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts). The 15% basic rate also applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by CCPCs and ECPCs in excess of their annual expenditure limit.

The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35%—calculated under subsection 127(10.1) as the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement—is available on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit ($6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024) for two classes of corporations:

items: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), whether stand-alone or associated.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), as defined in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must be a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange, be resident in Canada, and not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons. Furthermore, even if all the shares owned by non-residents were hypothetically owned by a single particular person, the corporation must still not be controlled by that particular person.

body.text: Several statutory rules govern the application of this refundability matrix. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit is $3,000,000 per year; for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit is $6,000,000 per year. Depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024 (including property deemed acquired before December 16, 2024, under available-for-use rules) cannot be claimed for SR&ED purposes. Depreciable capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024, qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, with refundability capped at 40% under subsection 127.1(2.01).

A Qualifying Corporation is defined under subsection 127.1(2) as a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their taxation years ending in the same calendar year) did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit for the current taxation year. Under the CRA Glossary and the ITA, the Qualifying Income Limit is determined by the formula:

In this formula, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, A is nil if the corporation's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined with that of its associated corporations) is less than or equal to $15,000,000; in any other case, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Because post-2010 federal rules removed the prior-year taxable income test from the primary expenditure limit calculation, a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeds its Qualifying Income Limit ("Other CCPCs" in the third row of the table above) still earns the 100% refundable 35% ITC on current expenditures (and 40% refundable on capital expenditures) up to its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, losing only the 40% refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit.
2.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Group Allocation Rules
1. CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's baseline $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once its taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with all associated corporations) reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically under amended subsection 127(10.2):

In this formula, A equals $0 if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated corporations) is less than or equal to $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Consequently, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the expenditure limit was $3,000,000 and phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital.)
2. ECPC and Electing CCPC Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32))

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(10.6)—as well as stand-alone CCPCs electing under subsection 127(10.31) and associated CCPC groups electing under subsection 127(10.32) to use the revenue method in lieu of the taxable capital method—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced based on the average annual revenue of the 3 preceding fiscal years. The reduction begins when the three-year average annual revenue reaches $15,000,000, and the expenditure limit becomes nil starting at $75,000,000.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), for ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group, the revenue phase-out is calculated using the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements (as defined in subsection 233.8(1) of the ITA) of the group for the preceding 3 fiscal years; if an ECPC has fewer than 3 preceding fiscal years, the average is based on the actual number of fiscal years. For CCPCs electing into the revenue method under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32), the calculation uses total average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each group member for the preceding 3 fiscal years (regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout the entire three-year period), includes the corporation's reasonable share of annual revenue from any partnership or trust, and allows reasonable adjustments (such as eliminating intra-group sales) so that annual revenue reflects a single economic entity.
3. Associated CCPCs, Consolidated ECPCs, Short Tax Years, and Multiple Tax Years

Where a CCPC is associated with one or more other corporations, subsection 127(10.21) provides that its default expenditure limit for a taxation year is nil unless the associated group files an agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3) (or the prescribed schedule for revenue-electing CCPCs under subsection 127(10.32)) to allocate the group expenditure limit among the members. If an associated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days after a ministerial request, the Minister of National Revenue allocates the limit under subsection 127(10.4). Paralleling these CCPC rules, subsection 127(10.61) sets the default expenditure limit of a consolidated ECPC member to nil unless the consolidated group files an allocation election under subsection 127(10.62) (with ministerial allocation after 30 days under subsection 127(10.63)).
If a corporation's taxation year is less than 51 weeks (a short taxation year), its expenditure limit is prorated using the formula set out in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy:
Prorated Expenditure Limit = Expenditure Limit × (Number of Days in the Taxation Year ÷ 365)

Furthermore, subsections 127(10.5) and 127(10.64) govern the determination of the expenditure limit when a corporation has two or more taxation years ending in the same calendar year and is associated or consolidated with another corporation that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year. As illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy example for associated CCPCs Corporation P (June 30 year-end changing to December 31 in 2027) and Corporation Q (December 31 year-end) splitting a $6,000,000 group limit equally ($3,000,000 each), the second short taxation year in 2027 is prorated based on days:

cells: Prorated for 6-month (184-day) short period: $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) under s. 127(10.5)

body.text: 2.4 Carryforward/Carryback Periods, Section 37 Pool Adjustments, and Loss Restriction Events
1. ITC Carryback and Carryforward Periods (Subsection 127(9))

Unused non-refundable federal SR&ED ITCs—or any portion of an earned ITC remaining after reducing Part I federal income tax payable to zero and claiming available cash refunds—may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable. Any ITC that is not applied within the 20-tax-year carryforward window expires permanently. Moreover, ITCs earned on repayments of government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments under subsection 127(9) are calculated using the ITC rate that applied in the year the assistance originally reduced the expenditure base; while these repayment ITCs are non-refundable in the year of repayment, they may be applied against current Part I tax, carried back 3 years, or carried forward 20 years.
2. Section 37 Pool Mechanics and Taxability of Credits

The Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures operates as an indefinite running balance tracked in Part 3, Section C of Form T661. Claimants have the option of deducting all, part, or none of the available positive pool balance in a given taxation year, carrying forward any unclaimed balance indefinitely without expiration.

The pool balance is increased each taxation year by six statutory additions: allowable current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada in the year (paragraph 37(1)(a), Line 380); allowable capital SR&ED expenditures on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390); repayments of government or non-government assistance made in the year to the extent the assistance had previously reduced the pool (paragraph 37(1)(c), Line 445); negative pool balances included in income in the preceding taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) (paragraph 37(1)(c.1)); prior-year federal SR&ED ITC recapture amounts (paragraph 37(1)(c.2), Line 453); and pool balances transferred from predecessor corporations upon an amalgamation (section 87) or wind-up (section 88).
Conversely, the Section 37 pool balance is decreased each taxation year by four statutory reductions:

items: Government and Non-Government Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(d), Lines 429–432): All government and non-government assistance (including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, unless formally renounced on time, but excluding the portion of a provincial credit attributable to the PPA under the proxy method) that the claimant received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date.

Prior-Year Federal SR&ED ITCs Applied or Refunded (Paragraph 37(1)(e), Line 435): Any federal SR&ED ITC used in the immediately preceding taxation year—whether refunded in cash, applied against Part I tax payable, or carried back to a prior year—reduces the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the current taxation year. If the prior-year ITC reduction (or current-year assistance) results in a negative balance in the Section 37 pool at the end of a taxation year, that negative amount must be brought directly into the taxpayer's net business income for tax purposes in that taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v), and the opening pool balance for the following taxation year is reset to nil. (For partnerships, because a partnership is prohibited from carrying forward a Section 37 pool under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and must fully deduct its available pool balance at the partnership level in the year incurred, the federal ITC allocated to partners reduces the partnership's Section 37 pool in the same taxation year rather than the following year, and partners do not include partnership-allocated ITCs on Line 435.)

body.text: Additionally, under subsection 37(4) and ITR paragraph 2902(c), no deduction or ITC is permitted for an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (preventing duplication of tax incentives between performer and purchaser or claiming rights to foreign R&D). Under subsection 37(5), any expenditure in respect of SR&ED that could qualify as both an SR&ED expenditure and a charitable donation under section 110.1 or 118.1 must be deducted exclusively under Section 37 as an SR&ED expenditure.
3. Loss Restriction Events / Acquisition of Control (Subsection 37(6.1))

When a corporation undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of corporate control, or a change in majority-interest beneficiaries for a trust), a deemed taxation year-end occurs immediately prior to the event, reducing the taxpayer's unrestricted Section 37 pool to nil under subsection 37(6.1) (amended by Bill C-15 via clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B) to encompass restored capital expenditures and property under paragraph 37(1)(b) acquired on or after December 16, 2024) and restricting the carryforward and carryback of unused Section 127 ITCs. In subsequent taxation years, the pre-acquisition Section 37 pool balance (and pre-acquisition unused ITCs) may be reinstated and deducted only if (1) the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and (2) the deduction is claimed only to the extent of income for that taxation year derived from that same business or a similar business (calculated before making any Section 37 pool deduction).
Section 3: Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Specific Cost Rules
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subsection 37(10) and ITR Section 2900)

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, a claimant must elect on Form T661 (Part 3, Line 160) for each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). This election is made on a year-by-year basis and is irrevocable for that taxation year once the claim is filed; if a claimant does not select a method on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method by default.
Mechanics of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and the Overall Proxy Cap

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate actual SR&ED overhead and other indirect expenditures on Form T661 (instead deducting those actual overhead expenses as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA). In their place, the claimant computes a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 to include in Section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 502) for earning ITCs. Since the 2014 calendar year, ITR subsection 2900(4) sets the PPA at 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (reduced from 60% in 2013 and 65% in 2012 and prior years).

To ensure that the total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specified deductions do not exceed the total business expenditures actually deducted by the taxpayer in the year, ITR subsection 2900(6) subjects the PPA to an Overall Cap calculated by the formula:
Overall Cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A represents the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold). B represents the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (such as CCA, interest, and bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents and brokers), Section 37 (the SR&ED expenditure pool deduction per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts). C represents the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as facility rent). In practice, the Overall Cap does not restrict the calculated 55% PPA if the claimant has deducted more than $55 of eligible non-SR&ED business expenses for every $100 of eligible salary included in the salary base.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages (Subsection 248(1), Subsection 37(8), and CRA Salary or Wages Policy)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA (and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA (Sections 5 to 8). Dividends, shareholder draws, unpaid founder time, and consulting fees paid to independent contractors do not constitute salary or wages.
1. Qualifying Tasks ("Directly Engaged"), Inclusions, and Exclusions

Whether an employee's remuneration qualifies depends strictly on the actual technical tasks performed and time tracked, never on the employee's job title. Under the Proxy Method (and for direct hands-on labour under the Traditional Method), "directly engaged" in SR&ED covers seven specific hands-on duties:

items: Hands-on experimentation and scientific or technical analysis.

The eight statutory support work categories under paragraph 248(1)(d)—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research—when commensurate with the needs and directly in support of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

Supervised non-specialized tasks (such as machine operators feeding raw materials or operating machinery for experiments), provided the work is an integral part of the SR&ED and is directly supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications.

First-line technical supervision, SR&ED contract administration, and technical coordination by managers who direct ongoing technical work or provide direct technical input (excluding higher-level executives making non-technological or business decisions).
Technical planning for ongoing, claimed SR&ED projects.
Technical feasibility studies directly related to claimed SR&ED projects.
Preparation of internal technical documentation recording the SR&ED work.

body.text: In computing allowable SR&ED salary or wages, claimants may include regular base pay, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, normal sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, gratuities, honorariums, director's or management fees, commissions, inducements, non-competition payments, bonuses and remuneration based on profits (only for non-specified employees), and taxable benefits under Section 6. Taxable benefits may include cash outlays or reasonable estimates of non-cash benefits, provided the actual costs are not deducted elsewhere as a business expense and excluding any GST/HST or PST component for which the employer can claim an input tax credit or rebate, as input tax credits are deemed to be government assistance under subsection 248(16). Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages under both methods exclude the employer's share of payroll and related benefits (such as CPP, QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, approved pension or superannuation plans, and medical/dental insurance, though these may be claimed as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method for hands-on SR&ED staff), stock option benefits under Section 7, retiring allowances, and extended vacation or extended sick leave beyond normal annual leave.
2. Specified Employees: The 5 × YMPE Pool Cap and 75% / 2.5 × YMPE Proxy Cap

A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee of a corporation who is either a specified shareholder—owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, sibling, or other related family member of a controlling shareholder). Under the constructive ownership rules highlighted in CloudAcc's 2026 founder guide, shares owned by non-arm's length persons count toward the individual's threshold, shares held through a partnership or fixed trust count in proportion to the individual's interest, and beneficiaries of a discretionary family trust are deemed to own 100% of the trust's shares; furthermore, holding 10% or more at any time in the taxation year triggers specified employee status for that entire taxation year, even if the founder is diluted below 10% during a subsequent financing round.
Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions under the ITA and ITR:

First, under subsection 37(9) of the ITA, any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is completely excluded from allowable SR&ED expenditures (Line 305) under both the Traditional and Proxy methods.

Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed in Part 3 of Form T661 for a specified employee (after multiplying eligible salary by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED, up to 100%) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year the individual was a specified employee:
Maximum Specified Employee Salary or Wages = 5 × YMPE × (Number of Days in the Taxation Year the Individual Was a Specified Employee ÷ 365)

As illustrated in CloudAcc's 2026 guide, based on a YMPE of $74,600, the 5 × YMPE cap equals $373,000 for a full 365-day taxation year. Under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, zero salary counts across any of them unless all associated corporations file an agreement using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) to allocate a single shared 5 × YMPE cap among themselves.

Third, when computing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661, ITR subsection 2900(9) first excludes bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year from the proxy salary base for all employees (both non-specified and specified) on Line 812 and Line 852. Next, ITR subsection 2900(7) restricts the maximum amount that can be included in the proxy salary base (Lines 850–860) for a specified employee to the lesser of (1) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages)—meaning that even if a founder devotes 100% of their time to SR&ED and claims 100% of their salary in Part 3, their Part 5 proxy salary base is capped at 75%—or (2) 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual:
Specified Employee Proxy Salary Base Cap = 2.5 × YMPE × (Number of Days in the Taxation Year the Claimant Employed the Individual ÷ 365)

Based on a YMPE of $74,600, 2.5 × YMPE equals $186,500 for a full year. Under ITR subsection 2900(8) (and deemed association rules in ITR subsection 2900(10)), this 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base cap must be shared once across all associated corporations employing the specified employee in taxation years ending in the same calendar year.
3. Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2))

While SR&ED expenditures must generally be incurred for work carried on inside Canada (which includes Canada's exclusive economic zone under subsection 37(1.3)), subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA permit a claimant to include "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada in both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures (as well as the PPA salary base), subject to strict qualitative criteria and a 10% statutory ceiling.

Under subsection 37(1.4) and CRA policy, four qualitative conditions must be met: the work must be directly undertaken by an employee of the taxpayer (foreign work by subcontractors never qualifies for ITCs); the employee must be a Canadian resident at the time the expense is incurred; the foreign SR&ED work must relate to a business of the taxpayer and be an integral part of, and solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer; and the salary or wages paid must not be subject to an income or profits tax from another country. Under subsection 37(1.5), the total permissible outside-Canada salary and wages claimed in a taxation year (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees, with Line 265 checked in Part 2) is limited to 10% of the total SR&ED salary and wages incurred for SR&ED performed in Canada during that taxation year. Separately, subsection 37(2) permits a current income deduction (but 0% Section 127 ITC and no addition to the subsection 37(1) pool) for current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada, including payments to approved foreign universities such as Harvard University and the University of North Dakota under paragraph 37(2)(b).
4. The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule: Wages vs. Other Current Expenditures (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

The ITA enforces a strict 180-day payment window following the end of the taxation year for accrued expenses, applying distinct statutory mechanisms to unpaid wages versus unpaid non-wage current expenditures.

For Unpaid Salaries and Wages (Subsection 78(4) and Subsection 127(26)), if accrued employee remuneration incurred in Taxation Year 1 is not actually paid within 180 days from the end of Taxation Year 1, subsection 78(4) deems the expenditure not to have been incurred in Taxation Year 1 for both the Section 37 pool of deductible expenditures and Section 127 qualified expenditures. The claimant must deduct the unpaid wages on Line 315 of Form T661 in Year 1; when the remuneration is subsequently paid in a later taxation year, it is treated as incurred in that payment year and claimed on Line 310, though it remains permanently excluded from the Part 5 proxy salary base under ITR subsection 2900(9).

For Unpaid Non-Wage Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26)), if a current expenditure other than salary or wages (such as an arm's length SR&ED contractor invoice or material outlay) is incurred in Taxation Year 1 but remains unpaid 180 days after the end of Taxation Year 1, the expenditure remains included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in Year 1. However, for Section 127 ITC purposes, subsection 127(26) excludes the unpaid amount from qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 in Year 1 (for an unpaid arm's length SR&ED contract, a 20% reduction is first taken on Line 529 and the remaining 80% unpaid balance is deducted on Line 520). When the liability is actually paid in a subsequent taxation year, it is added back to qualified expenditures on Line 500 (at 80% for contract expenditures)—provided and only provided that the unpaid amount was originally identified on Form T661 within the statutory 18-month reporting deadline for Year 1.
3.3 Subcontractors (Arm's Length vs. Non-Arm's Length) and Third-Party Payments
1. Arm's Length vs. Non-Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts

When a claimant contracts another party to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), tax treatment bifurcates based on whether the parties deal at arm's length under Section 251 of the ITA.

For Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure (for basic research, applied research, experimental development, or commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf) is included in the Section 37 deductible pool, while 80% is included in Section 127 qualified expenditures to earn ITCs (via a 20% statutory reduction under subparagraph 127(9)(a)(ii) reported on Line 529 of Form T661), provided the contractor is a "taxable supplier" (payments to non-taxable suppliers are removed on Line 528). If a single contract combines SR&ED and commercial work, the price must be reasonably allocated based on fair market value, and prepaid amounts for work not yet performed are disallowed in the year under subsection 18(9). Notably, while an arm's length performer contracted solely to perform support work (such as testing or machining) cannot claim SR&ED ITCs on its own tax return because support work alone does not meet the definition of SR&ED, the payer/claimant is entitled to claim 80% of that contract expenditure provided the support work is commensurate with and directly supports the payer's Canadian SR&ED project. Furthermore, consequential on restoring capital expenditures, Bill C-15 repealed the former subsection 37(14) and 37(15) capital look-through rules effective for property acquired or leased on or after December 16, 2024.

For Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Paragraph 127(9)(f), Subsection 127(13), and Subsection 127(24)), payments to an NAL contractor for SR&ED performed on the payer's behalf are allowable in the payer's Section 37 deductible pool, but are excluded from the payer's Section 127 qualified expenditures and earn 0% ITCs directly for the payer (paragraph 127(9)(f)). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures, and the amount received from the NAL payer is not treated as a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) (so it does not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures). Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and payer may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or a portion of the performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer (reported on Line 508 for the transferee and Line 544 for the transferor; note that partnerships cannot use Form T1146). Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), a claimant cannot circumvent NAL restrictions by interposing an arm's length intermediary between itself and an NAL performer if the main purpose is to generate a qualified expenditure. Additionally, where a claimant purchases goods (materials or capital property) or non-SR&ED services from an NAL supplier, subsection 127(11.6) restricts the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier, stripping out any intercompany profit markup (adjusted on Lines 541, 542, and 543 of Form T661).
2. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) & Form T1263)

Unlike an SR&ED contract where the work is controlled by the payer, rights are exclusive to a single payer, and tax accounting follows an accrual basis, a third-party payment is a contribution (direct cash funding, funding of students/employees, or payments in kind valued at fair market value) where the SR&ED is controlled by the external performer, rights are non-exclusive (though the claimant must hold a preferential right or entitlement to exploit the results in its business), and accounting generally follows a cash basis. Like arm's length contracts, 100% of an eligible third-party payment enters the Section 37 pool and 80% qualifies for Section 127 ITCs (20% reduction on Line 529), and the claimant must attach a completed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment. 3.4 Materials, Production Runs, Custom Assets, and 20-Year ITC Recapture
1. Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) & (B)(V) and ITR 2900(2)(a))

To qualify as materials for SR&ED (100% eligible under both Traditional and Proxy methods in the taxation year actually consumed or transformed), items must be physical and tangible substances (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is performed or which results from the SR&ED, including laid-down acquisition costs (invoice cost, transportation, customs/excise duties, and direct labour/production overhead for internally manufactured inputs). Materials Consumed are items destroyed, absorbed, broken down, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED process or testing (such as chemical reagents, ink in a printing test, or metal parts destroyed in stress testing); materials consumed are permanently eligible and never subject to ITC recapture. Materials Transformed are items changed or incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom product, or commercial asset during SR&ED that retains some commercial or resale value after testing concludes; materials transformed are 100% claimable in the year transformed, but are subject to ITC recapture if the resulting property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years.
2. SR&ED During Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP) and Developing Commercial Assets
When experimental development takes place in a manufacturing plant or commercial facility, the CRA applies two specialized administrative policies.

First, under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, every production run involving SR&ED must be classified as either Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) or Experimental Development in Conjunction with Commercial Production (ED+CP). A run qualifies as ED+EP only when its primary purpose is to evaluate technical aspects of an SR&ED project and genuine technical risk exists to the process or product due to technological uncertainties (such as operating outside normal parameter ranges with risk of process instability, output inconsistencies, production stoppages, equipment damage, or abnormal yield loss, supported by advance experimental operating instructions and senior management authorization of technical risk) with no simultaneous commercial work. Under ED+EP, 100% of the labour, material, and overhead costs of the required experimental production run are allowable, excluding any excess production beyond the quantity strictly required to validate the SR&ED hypothesis. Conversely, ED+CP is the default classification when experimental trials take place simultaneously with commercial production while process indicators are monitored to prevent adverse effects on product quality or process stability. Under ED+CP, regular commercial production costs are non-allowable; only incremental costs (such as additional engineering supervision, incremental downtime, or incremental material loss exceeding standard operational loss) qualify as SR&ED expenditures.

Second, under the SR&ED While Developing an Asset Policy, the CRA distinguishes between a pilot plant—a non-commercial scale facility developed for the primary purpose of conducting SR&ED over its useful life and isolated from commercial operations (where all development and operating costs qualify, excluding buildings; if designed for temporary or permanent conversion to commercial operations, it is a commercial plant rather than a pilot plant)—and custom products or commercial assets. For custom products or commercial assets combining SR&ED and commercial components, only the SR&ED components and closely interrelated redesigned components qualify. Where it is impossible to isolate SR&ED work from commercial construction costs on a custom asset, the CRA permits an Alternative Incremental Cost Approach—provided the CRA agrees to its use and the claimant signs a formal waiver of objection and appeal rights under subsection 169(2.2) of the ITA—calculated as:

Allowable SR&ED Expenditure = (Total Actual Cost of Developing the Custom Product or Commercial Asset − Estimated Cost Had the Technology Already Existed) + Estimated Cost of Materials Transformed in SR&ED

As illustrated in the CRA's policy example, if a custom machine costs $150,000 to build, would have cost $125,000 had the technology already existed, and incorporates $30,000 of materials transformed in SR&ED, the allowable SR&ED expenditure is ($150,000 − $125,000) + $30,000 = $55,000, with the $30,000 of transformed materials subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial use.
3. Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA (and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy), if a claimant acquires or transforms property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned—specifically materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (when converted ASA to commercial use), animals and growing things, or property acquired under an SR&ED contract—and subsequently sells the property or converts it to commercial use within 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)), the claimant must recapture the ITC.

For an arm's length sale, the recapture equals the lesser of (1) the original ITC earned on the qualified expenditure for the property, and (2) the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value [FMV] at the time of commercial conversion or non-arm's length disposition; for SUE, 25% or 50% of proceeds/FMV under subclauses 127(27)(f)(ii)(B) and (C)) multiplied by the ITC rate (such as 35% or 15%) at which the credit was originally earned. Crucially, if a component is manufactured in-house, only the cost of materials transformed is subject to recapture (in-house salaries and overhead are never recaptured); however, if the component is purchased or contracted from an arm's length supplier (for instance, a $12,000 supplier contract comprising $10,000 manufacturing/development cost plus $2,000 supplier profit), the entire $12,000 price is "cost" under subsection 127(32) and subject to recapture. The recaptured ITC is added directly to Part I federal income tax payable in the year of sale or conversion (via Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)), and an equivalent amount is added back to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) (Line 453 of Form T661). Under subsections 127(33) to 127(35), non-arm's length transfers of SR&ED capital property during corporate reorganizations defer immediate recapture provided the transferee continues to use the property for SR&ED.
3.5 Overhead and Other Expenditures (Traditional Method Only)

Claimants electing the Traditional Method may claim overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and ITR paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3), provided each expense satisfies two mandatory "Directly Attributable" tests:

items: The Directly Related Test: The expenditure must connect directly—without an intervening step or intermediary—to (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery and equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The Incremental Test: The expenditure (or claimed incremental portion) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

body.text: Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, salaries and wages of clerical and administrative staff (such as HR, accounting, and purchasing personnel) providing a non-technological service directly aiding ongoing SR&ED employees qualify on Line 360 if directly related and incremental; however, their associated payroll benefits, training costs, retiring allowances, and travel expenses are disallowed because their link to SR&ED work is indirect. Conversely, the employer's share of related benefits and retiring allowances (allocated based on career SR&ED wage ratios) for hands-on SR&ED employees may qualify if directly related and incremental. For personnel recruitment, headhunter fees, job advertising, selection travel, and immigration/work permit/visa costs are disallowed as SR&ED overhead (deductible only as regular business expenses), whereas moving/relocation expenses (subsection 62(3)) and employee housing-loss taxable benefits (subsections 6(19) and 6(20)) to relocate selected SR&ED candidates or transfer SR&ED personnel to another facility within Canada qualify for both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 ITCs.
3.6 Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024 Restoration)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15, the CRA published updated versions of the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026 / October 7, 2026) governing capital and lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024.
1. ASA Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) & (B)(III), and Subsection 37(1.2))

Capital expenditures qualify under paragraph 37(1)(b) when made to acquire depreciable property (property owned by the claimant or in which the claimant holds a leasehold interest eligible for CCA under paragraph 20(1)(a)) that is acquired and available for use (under subsection 37(1.2) and subsection 13(27), the earliest of when first used to earn income/perform SR&ED or when delivered and capable of producing a commercially saleable product or service) after December 15, 2024. At the time of acquisition, the claimant must satisfy the All or Substantially All (ASA, defined as ≥90%) Intent Test: intending either to use the property during ≥90% of its operating time in its expected useful life in SR&ED carried on in Canada, or to consume ≥90% of its value in SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Allowable ASA capital expenditures are claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 (with the 10 most expensive capital properties listed per project on Lines 262 and 263, and the full capital cost including installation, freight, and customs/excise duties entered in Box 782). Because 100% of the capital cost enters the Section 37 SR&ED pool (and is deemed CCA allowed under amended subsection 37(6)), the asset must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). Crucially, while both new and used depreciable property meeting the ≥90% ASA test qualify for the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 390), used depreciable property (and costs to refurbish used property) is a prescribed expenditure under ITR paragraph 2902(b) that is excluded from Section 127 qualified expenditures (deducted on Line 532 of Form T661) and therefore earns 0% ITCs. Finally, non-depreciable property (land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, goodwill), property used outside Canada, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraph 37(8)(e) (except a prescribed special-purpose building under ITR section 2903).
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE - Subsection 127(9) and ITR Subsection 2900(11))

Depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA intent test may still generate partial Section 127 ITCs as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 (listing the 20 most expensive SUE items in Box 792) under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. To qualify as SUE, the property must be new depreciable property (never previously used or rented for any purpose prior to acquisition); must not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators; note that computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not GPOEF and qualify for SUE); and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under ITR subsection 2900(11) (which excludes buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, equipment intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its expected useful life under paragraph 2900(11)(d), and equipment intended to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or line and primarily for commercial use thereafter under paragraph 2900(11)(c)).
Unlike the ASA capital test (which is based on intent at acquisition), SUE qualification is evaluated based on actual operating time across two statutory periods:

items: First-Term SUE (25% Capital Cost Inclusion): The equipment is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period, which begins when the equipment is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that acquisition time. If met, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (calculated without borrowing costs under Section 21 or deemed capital cost rules under subsections 13(7.1) and 13(7.4), and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)) is deemed a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes at the end of that taxation year.

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% Capital Cost Inclusion): Provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE, if its cumulative actual operating time remains primarily (>50%) for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period—which begins on the acquisition date and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that acquisition time—an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC at the end of that second taxation year, for a combined qualified expenditure of up to 50% of capital cost across the two periods.

Section 4: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (2025–2026)

In addition to federal SR&ED incentives, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D credits are administered directly by the CRA via schedules attached to the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (or T1 Individual Return) and piggyback on the federal Form T661 definition of eligible SR&ED and qualified expenditures.
