body.text: 4.2 Detailed Analysis of Major Provincial R&D Regimes
1. Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario operates a three-tier corporate R&D tax credit system under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered by the CRA.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC - Section 96, Schedule 566) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (plus eligible repayments) up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (generating a maximum refundable credit of $240,000, shared across an associated corporate group and prorated by days over 365 for short taxation years). Unlike the federal SR&ED regime—which increased its expenditure limit to $6,000,000 and expanded its taxable capital phase-out to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 under Bill C-15—Ontario retained its $3,000,000 OITC cap and its existing dual phase-out thresholds. Specifically, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out linearly when the prior-year federal taxable income of the corporation and its associated corporations lies between $500,000 and $800,000, or when the prior-year specified capital amount of the corporation and its associated corporations lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Consequently, qualified Ontario SR&ED spending between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000 earns the 35% federal ITC (and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC), but 0% OITC. However, Ontario did harmonize with the federal restoration of capital expenditures: 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, qualify for both the OITC and the ORDTC, whereas capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, earn 0% in Ontario.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC - Sections 38–45, Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (net of the OITC and other government assistance) with no expenditure limit and no income or capital phase-out. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and forward 20 years against Ontario corporate income tax. Because the CRA treats an earned ORDTC—even when unused and carried forward in a loss year—as government assistance "reasonably expected to be received" under subsection 127(18) that immediately reduces the federal 35% refundable ITC base, an unprofitable Ontario CCPC can formally waive/renounce its current-year ORDTC (or OITC under subsection 96(14)) in writing with its return on or before 6 months after its taxation year-end (or on an amended return) to preserve its 35% cash refund from the federal SR&ED program.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC - Section 97, Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified expenditures paid under an eligible contract with an Ontario Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute, excluding salaries paid to institute employees connected to the claimant), up to an annual cap of $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures ($4,000,000 maximum credit, allocated among associated corporations).
2. Québec: The New CRIC Regime (Taxation Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

In its 2025–2026 Budget (tabled March 25, 2025), the Québec government enacted a comprehensive reform of its innovation tax system by introducing the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization / Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation (CRIC). Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC replaced eight legacy Québec R&D tax credits (including the former R&D salary and wage credit [which had offered a 14% basic rate and up to 30% for qualifying SMEs], the university/public research centre credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, and the research consortium fee credit).

Unlike the legacy Québec system and the federal SR&ED system, CRIC credit rates are based on a corporation's volume of eligible spending rather than corporate size or CCPC status. Any corporation that operates a business in Québec, maintains an establishment there, and undertakes (or causes to be undertaken on its behalf) eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec receives a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier.

While CRIC's core R&D definition is harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) (with the CRA conducting the scientific review of R&D work), CRIC expands the provincial tax base to cover pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities encompass three areas: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; (2) product design, including form and aesthetic development, improved functionality, and material selection; and (3) quality control activities strictly limited to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial regulatory approval or certification.

Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work in Québec; 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for eligible contracts carried out in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and capital property acquisition costs for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (excluding land, buildings, and rights to use land or buildings; cannot be double-claimed with Québec's C3i investment and innovation credit or large investment project tax holidays). Before applying the 30% and 20% rates, total qualified expenditures must exceed an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax Basic Personal Amount ($18,751 in 2025) for each employee, prorated by the time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. Corporations claim the CRIC by filing Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (alongside Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated group expenditure limit agreements and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for the pre-commercialization component). (Additionally, as noted by GrantCompass, for fiscal years beginning in 2026, Québec replaced its legacy CDAE e-business tax credit with the CDAEIA AI adoption tax credit, whose refundable portion starts at 22% in 2026 and steps down toward 20% by 2028.)
3. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Atlantic / Northern Regimes

In British Columbia (Form T666 & Bill 2, 2026), under Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), the provincial government eliminated the former September 1, 2027 sunset clause to make the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent, and harmonized with federal Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: extending the 10% refundable credit to both CCPCs and ECPCs, doubling the refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits), raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, and restoring capital expenditures.

In Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant [IEG] - AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970), administered by Alberta TRA under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, qualified corporations receive an 8% base refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 years), and a 20% enhanced refundable payment (8% base + 12% incremental) on eligible Alberta R&D spending exceeding that base spending level, on up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending (filing deadline is 15 months after the corporation's filing due date).

In Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the province doubled the CCPC 10% refundable expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (maintaining a one-third ratio to the $6,000,000 federal limit), while expenditures above $2,000,000 and those incurred by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit, subject to a yearly maximum cap of $1,000,000 in combined refundable and non-refundable credits.

In Manitoba (Schedule T2SCH380), the 15% credit is 50% refundable (an effective 7.5% refundable credit and 7.5% non-refundable credit with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward) for in-house R&D, and 100% refundable (15%) when R&D is conducted under contract with a qualifying institute. Finally, Nova Scotia (Schedule T2SCH340), New Brunswick (Schedule T2SCH360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule T2SCH301 / Form T1129), and Yukon (Schedule T2SCH442 / Form T1232) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap; uniquely, Newfoundland and Labrador does not reduce its eligible expenditure base by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits), although the resulting NL credit still reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure pools.
Section 5: Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Multi-Program Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Statutory Reduction Rules for Assistance and Contract Payments

To ensure that SR&ED tax incentives apply only to a claimant's net out-of-pocket R&D expenditure, the ITA enforces reduction rules under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(11.1), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) (as set out in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy).

Government Assistance is defined under subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (an entity with a public duty, significant government control, and public-benefit profit dedication, including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect government funding via non-profit organizations) in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan (including conditional loans whose repayment depends on future revenues or profits), deduction from tax, or investment allowance—including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and provincial super-allowance benefit amounts, but excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Non-Government Assistance is defined as any amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) received as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance for the cost of property or an outlay/expense. Contract Payments are amounts paid or payable by an arm's length taxable supplier for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to a Section 37 deduction, or payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity (Section 149) for SR&ED to be performed on its behalf. Where a claimant conducts R&D on its own account at its own financial risk and merely sells a deliverable product or service under a commercial engagement, the receipt is commercial revenue rather than a contract payment.

Assistance and contract payments are recognized on an accrual basis in the taxation year in which the claimant has "received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive" the amount on or before the income tax return filing due date. Assistance reduces the Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures on a project-by-project basis down to a floor of nil; excess assistance on one project does not reduce another independent project unless transferred across non-arm's length parties under subsections 127(19) and 127(20) via Form T1145.
5.2 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Assistance Nuance

A critical audit distinction governs how provincial and territorial R&D tax credits interact with the federal Section 37 pool versus Section 127 qualified expenditures under the Proxy Method (Section 4.5 of the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy).

Under the Traditional Method, 100% of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as Ontario's OITC/ORDTC or BC's SR&ED credit) reduces both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(d), Line 429) and Section 127 qualified expenditures (subsection 127(18), Line 513/514). Under the Proxy Method, however, provincial R&D credits (outside Québec) are calculated on a base that includes both direct expenditures and the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Because the PPA is not an expenditure included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, the portion of the provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the PPA does not reduce the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool on Line 429; instead, that PPA-related portion of the provincial credit must be included directly in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the taxation year it is received or applied. For Section 127 federal ITC calculation purposes, however, 100% of the provincial or territorial R&D tax credit (including both the direct expenditure portion and the PPA portion) reduces Section 127 qualified expenditures on Line 513. Similarly, in Québec, any portion of a Québec R&D credit earned on salaries for work that assists R&D (which is excluded under the federal proxy method) is not government assistance for the federal Section 37 pool, but is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received.

Assume a Québec CCPC (with prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000) incurs $2,000,000 of eligible hands-on R&D salaries in Québec during a taxation year beginning after March 25, 2025, elects the federal Proxy Method (55% PPA), and has an applicable CRIC Exclusion Threshold of $50,000. First, on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, the $2,000,000 qualified salary base is reduced by the $50,000 exclusion threshold to yield $1,950,000 of eligible spending above the threshold. Applying the 30% enhanced CRIC rate on the first $1,000,000 yields $300,000, and applying the 20% base CRIC rate on the remaining $950,000 yields $190,000, for a total fully refundable Québec CRIC of $490,000. Second, on federal Form T661, the $2,000,000 direct salary base plus the 55% PPA ($1,100,000) produces $3,100,000 of gross federal qualified expenditures. Deducting the $490,000 provincial CRIC assistance on Line 513 leaves $2,610,000 of net federal qualified expenditures, which at the 35% federal enhanced rate generates $913,500 in refundable federal ITC. Combined, the Québec CCPC recovers $1,403,500 in cash refunds ($490,000 CRIC + $913,500 federal SR&ED), representing 70.175% of its $2,000,000 R&D payroll outlay.
Worked Example 3: Stacking Federal Grants (NRC IRAP) and Clean Tech ITC with SR&ED

When a Canadian CCPC combines direct federal R&D grants—such as the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which reimburses up to 75%–80% of internal R&D labour and up to 50%–75% of subcontractor costs for incorporated Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer FTEs—with SR&ED and capital Investment Tax Credits, the grant reduces the eligible expenditure base under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18). Applying these rules to GrantCompass's 2026 clean technology funding model for a $500,000 project ($250,000 in R&D labour, $50,000 in additional R&D expenses/PPA net base, and $200,000 in Clean Technology capital equipment): routing the $250,000 labour to NRC IRAP at 80% yields a $200,000 grant; claiming the 35% enhanced SR&ED ITC on the $100,000 of remaining unassisted R&D expenses ($300,000 of R&D expenses less the $200,000 grant) yields $35,000; and claiming the 30% Clean Technology ITC on the $200,000 equipment purchase yields $60,000. In total, the company secures $295,000 (59% of the $500,000 project cost) in non-dilutive government funding, reducing its net cost to $205,000.
Section 6: Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Protocols
6.1 Governing Authorities and the Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

The federal SR&ED program is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates tax policy and legislative amendments under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which administers the program, conducts technical and financial reviews, and issues assessments and refunds).

Under subsection 37(11) (for Section 37 expenditure deductibility) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for Section 127 ITCs), a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred:

items: Corporations (Paragraph 150(1)(a)): A corporation's T2 return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year; adding 12 months establishes a statutory SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year. (If the tax year ends on the last day of a month, the return is due on the last day of the 6th month and the SR&ED claim is due on the last day of the 18th month; if it does not end on the last day of a month, the deadlines fall on the same day of the 6th and 18th months, respectively.)

Individuals / Sole Proprietorships: The T1 return filing due date is June 15 of the following calendar year, giving an individual until June 15 of the second following calendar year (17.5 months after a December 31 year-end) to file Form T661 and Form T2038(IND).
Trusts: The T3 return filing due date is 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end, resulting in an SR&ED reporting deadline of 15 months after the trust's taxation year-end.

Partnerships: Where SR&ED is performed by a partnership required to file a T5013 Partnership Information Return, Form T661 should be filed with the T5013 no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing due dates for the income tax returns of the partners for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends, and each partner must file Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) by that partner's respective SR&ED reporting deadline. (Note that under the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partnership ITC is calculated strictly at the 15% basic rate, cannot be allocated to a specified member [such as a limited partner or passive general partner, whose share is reallocated to active general partners unless renounced on Form T932 under subsection 127(8.4)], and any partnership loss created by deducting the Section 37 pool is disallowed to limited partners.)

body.text: 6.3 The CRA Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, enabling eligible businesses to obtain an upfront written eligibility determination from a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) before commencing work or incurring project costs:

items: Confirm Business and Project Eligibility: The applicant business must operate in Canada as a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA. The planned project must address a scientific or technological uncertainty through a systematic investigation, must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim, and must not involve issues currently under formal objection or litigation.

Request a Case Number and Submit Application via My Business Account: The claimant requests a case number on Canada.ca (received within 2 business days in My Business Account for existing SR&ED claimants, or following a CRA phone call within 5 business days for new claimants) and uploads the completed application and existing project plans in My Business Account for up to 3 projects.

Participate in the RTA Evaluation Meeting: The CRA assigns an RTA to evaluate the application. For new SR&ED claimants, a 2-to-5 hour meeting (virtual or on-site, which may include a virtual or physical facility tour) with the RTA is mandatory; for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, the RTA meeting is optional at the RTA's discretion.

Receive Written Determination Within 8 Weeks (Valid for Up to 3 Years): Within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application, the RTA issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If approved, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years (reported on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661 when filing the annual SR&ED claim), and if a refundable claim containing only pre-approved projects (without material changes) is selected for an expenditure review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

body.text: 6.4 CRA Review Procedures, Service Standards, Gross Negligence Penalties, and Appeals

Once a complete SR&ED claim and income tax return are received, the CRA applies three processing service standards to refundable claims (no service standard applies to non-refundable claims): 60 calendar days when accepted as filed without review; 90 calendar days when selected for an expenditure-only review where all claimed projects hold Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 calendar days (committed to 90% of the time) when selected for a technical and financial review. First-time claimants (or claimants that have not submitted a claim in the preceding 3 years) may also be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS). The normal reassessment period is 3 years from the original Notice of Assessment date for CCPCs and 4 years for non-CCPCs.

Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn, because Form T661 and its Part 10 certification form an integral part of the income tax return. Reviews are conducted jointly (primarily via virtual videoconferencing and electronic document transmission under national file assignment, or on-site on an exceptional basis) by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—who evaluates subsection 248(1) eligibility, interviews technical personnel, and authors the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report under a Research and Technology Manager (RTM)—and a Financial Reviewer (FR)—who audits expenditure allowability under a Financial Review Manager (FRM). Under subsection 230(1) of the ITA, books and records must be kept in an organized, usable form; if a claimant repeatedly ignores documentation requests, the RTA (after mandatory consultation with the RTM) and FR may issue a formal "Better Books and Records" letter requiring signed agreement within 30 days.

If adjustments are proposed at the conclusion of the review, the CRA issues a Proposal Package comprising the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and a Proposal Letter, giving the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations with additional facts or supporting evidence. Unresolved concerns follow the CRA's Three-Step Dispute Resolution Process: (1) speak directly with the RTA and/or FR; (2) escalate to the RTM and/or FRM; and (3) request a formal Administrative Review upon receiving the proposal package. Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 calendar days to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and if unresolved, may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

Finally, under subsection 163(2) of the ITA (specifically paragraphs 163(2)(a) and 163(2)(d), as detailed in the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy, updated January 28, 2025), if the CRA establishes on a balance of probabilities (subsection 163(3)) that a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (beyond simple oversight or misunderstanding), made or participated in a false statement or omission on an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the civil penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a)), plus (2) the entire refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed (paragraph 163(2)(d)).
Section 7: Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

In Canada, the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) is interpreted and enforced through a settled body of binding jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). Every SR&ED technical review and litigation defence is anchored in the Five-Question Test formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), where each of the five criteria must be answered in the affirmative:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? ("Routine engineering" refers to techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedure or routine engineering, no technological uncertainty exists).

Formulation of Specific Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (Justice Bowman specified that this involves a five-step process: observation of the subject matter of the problem; formulation of a clear objective; identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; formulation of a hypothesis designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and methodical and systematic testing of the hypothesis).

Accordance with the Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (Intuitive creativity and genius can play a vital role provided they operate within the discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experimentation).

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement? (Refers to achieving an advancement in general understanding among persons knowledgeable in the field; rejecting a hypothesis after systematic testing still constitutes an advancement because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis and defines technological boundaries).

Contemporaneous Record Keeping: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results kept as the work progressed? (Although not explicitly stated as a standalone clause in the Act or Regulations, Justice Bowman clarified that keeping a detailed record as work progresses is inherent to the statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation").

Legislative purpose of SR&ED incentives in evaluating industrial textile research.
Taxpayer appeal allowed. Held that the tax incentives given for doing SR&ED are intended to encourage scientific research in Canada and should be interpreted in light of that incentive purpose.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839
Eligibility of hydraulic physical modelling projects and the legal test for subsection 248(1).

Taxpayer appeal largely allowed. Justice Bowman established the landmark Five-Question Test (uncertainty, hypotheses, scientific method, technological advancement, and progressive record-keeping) that governs all Canadian SR&ED claims.
R I S - Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890
Evidentiary weight of documentary test records vs. oral testimony on repeatability of experiments.

Taxpayer appeal allowed. Approved Northwest Hydraulic at the appellate level; Justice Robertson held that while both documentary and viva voce evidence are admissible, documentary evidence of test data and results is the only sure means of establishing repeatable systematic investigation.
CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (aff'g 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC))
Post-hoc expert reconstruction of R&D vs. contemporaneous evidence.

Taxpayer appeal dismissed. Summarized and adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria at the FCA and highlighted the inadequacy of relying on post-hoc expert examination rather than contemporaneous records and testimony from personnel directly involved.
Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313
Whether a specific format of contemporaneous documentation is a legal condition precedent.

Clarified evidentiary standard (para. 94). Held that "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific content, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development" where credible evidence establishes the work.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Technological uncertainty in custom engineering and adequacy of internal engineering records.

Taxpayer appeal allowed. Demonstrated that technological uncertainty can exist where a known solution has never been used in a specific novel context, and contemporaneous records need not be designed for someone unfamiliar with the field to replicate results.
Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42, 2017 DTC 1022
Holistic project boundary evaluation vs. CRA's isolated task fragmentation on a pipe-liner mandrel project.

Taxpayer appeal allowed. Justice D'Auray rejected an overly narrow approach that reduced the mandrel project to isolated component tasks, holding that the project must be evaluated holistically in the context of the combined material and mechanical constraints.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88
Taxpayer challenge claiming the "scientific method" is not required because the words do not appear in s. 248(1).

Taxpayer appeal dismissed. The FCA rejected the argument that the scientific method is optional, reaffirming that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the settled judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)
Impact of CRA's 2021 Guidelines, "engineering method" vs. scientific method, and admissibility of expert reports.

Taxpayer appeal dismissed. Justice Rennie held that: (1) all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are mandatory; (2) CRA's 2021 Guidelines did not remove the scientific method and do not bind courts; and (3) a taxpayer-written expert report offering legal conclusions is inadmissible under White Burgess (2015 SCC 23).
Application of Northwest Hydraulic to food science and recipe/process modification (7 frozen pie projects, 2013–2016).

Taxpayer appeal allowed in full (all 7 projects). Chief Justice Rossiter rejected the CRA RTA's simplistic view ("A pie is a pie what is the big deal about it"), holding that Northwest Hydraulic must be applied in a context-sensitive, industry-appropriate manner.
Necessity of contemporaneous timesheets to prove SR&ED eligibility and labour allocation.

Reaffirmed flexible proof (para. 119). Held that although the CRA "would have liked to see contemporaneous time sheets for the work performed, they are not necessarily required for work to be eligible as qualifying SRED".

body.text: Key Audit Takeaways from Recent Jurisprudence

Three overarching legal principles emerge from the appellate and Tax Court of Canada decisions summarized above. First, adherence to the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria and the scientific method is mandatory across all industries (Kam-Press and National R&D). Taxpayers cannot argue that software development, sheet-metal fabrication, or applied engineering follows an "engineering method" exempt from the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (the scientific method). Even where the Tax Court accepts that genuine technological uncertainty existed (as in National R&D), the claim will be denied if the records are vague, unclear, and fail to reflect a methodical progression of explicit hypotheses, systematic testing, and logical conclusions linking the premise of each experiment to its empirical result.

Second, courts apply the Northwest Hydraulic test in a context-sensitive, holistic, and industry-appropriate manner (Canafric and Formadrain). Chief Justice Rossiter's ruling in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) and Justice D'Auray's ruling in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42) protect claimants against overly rigid or reductionist CRA reviews. An RTA cannot fragment an integrated engineering project into isolated sub-tasks to label each component "routine engineering" (Formadrain), nor can an RTA dismiss incremental food-science or manufacturing formulation experiments when interlocking commercial and physical constraints (such as simultaneous fat and salt reduction, ingredient replacement, shelf-life extension, and cooking-time reduction) create genuine technological uncertainty resolved through systematic trial modifications (Canafric).

Third, evidentiary discipline and expert witness independence are decisive in audit defence and litigation (Abeilles, DAZZM, and National R&D). Although Abeilles (2014 TCC 313) and DAZZM (2024 TCC 129) confirm that the absence of a specific document format (such as formal daily timesheets) does not automatically defeat an SR&ED claim at the Tax Court of Canada, claimants bear the legal burden of proof and should capture ordinary-course contemporaneous evidence—such as Git commit logs, ticket histories, sprint notes, lab notebooks, dated photographs, test logs, and payroll time allocations—as the work progresses (in accordance with Appendix 2 of Guide T4088). Finally, if a dispute proceeds to the Tax Court of Canada, National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) demonstrates that any expert witness must be strictly impartial and independent under White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co. (2015 SCC 23) and must confine their testimony to explaining technical context rather than usurping the court's function by opining on the legal question of whether the work constitutes SR&ED.
